mainTopic: Vows made under pressure to robbers and tax collectors, דינא דמלכותא דינא, and the start of a new משנה on conditional קרבן declarations
overview: This amud finishes a משנה about someone forced to make a vow to robbers or tax collectors to save his property. בית שמאי and בית הלל argue about whether he may use a שבועה, whether he may offer the vow first, and whether he may add more than he was asked. In every case בית הלל are more lenient. The גמרא then asks how one may mislead a tax collector when שמואל taught that the law of the kingdom is binding. It answers that the משנה means a collector with no fixed rate, or one who appointed himself. Next it explains how the vow that 'the produce is the king's' is worded: he says 'today' in his heart, and because he is forced, that unspoken limit counts. רב הונא then brings a ברייתא that seems to clash with the משנה about בית שמאי. The גמרא gives two answers, the second from רב אשי. Finally a new משנה begins about saplings or a garment declared a קרבן 'if not' or 'until' they are cut or burned, and its ruling on the 'until' case continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Can an oath be used to trick a robber?
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי allow any kind of vow except a שבועה; בית הלל allow even a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: [בית שמאי say: one may make vows to them in every form,] except by an oath. And בית הלל say: even by an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes the first argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל about vows forced out of a person by robbers or tax collectors. בית שמאי exclude a שבועה, and בית הלל permit even that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that one may make a misleading vow to save his property from a robber or tax collector. בית שמאי limit this: a נדר is allowed, but a שבועה is more serious and is not allowed. בית הלל say the pressure of the situation permits even a שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath; a person binds himself to do something or swears that something is true. It is more severe than a נדר.
The school of שמאי
The school of הלל
Even; this widens the rule to include more

steps.confusionAlert: This text starts in the middle of a sentence. The words 'except by an oath' belong to בית שמאי's ruling, which began on the previous דף.

phrases.english: except by an oath.
phrases.notes: This finishes בית שמאי's line from the previous דף: you may vow to robbers in every way except this one.

phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say: even by an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוּץ מִבִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the משנה's opening מחלוקת from the previous דף.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: a forced vow may be made in any form except a שבועה. בית הלל: even a שבועה is allowed.

steps.title: May he offer the vow before being asked?
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי say he should not start with a vow; בית הלל say he may start with one.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית שמאי say: he should not open with a vow for him. And בית הלל say: he may even open with one for him.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second argument. Should the person wait until the robber demands a vow, or may he offer one first?
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית שמאי allow the misleading vow only when it is truly needed, meaning when the robber asks for it. בית הלל allow the person to offer the vow on his own first, since the whole point is to save his property.

keyTerms.meaning: He will open, meaning he starts or offers first
A vow, usually one that makes something forbidden

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: לֹא יִפְתַּח לוֹ בְּנֶדֶר,
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: he should not open with a vow for him,
phrases.notes: He means: don't be the first to offer a vow. Only vow if the robber asks for one.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אַף יִפְתַּח לוֹ.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: he may even open with one for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: לֹא יִפְתַּח לוֹ בְּנֶדֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate disagreement on the same topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: vow only when asked. בית הלל: may offer the vow first.

steps.title: May he add more than the robber demanded?
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי allow vowing only on what he is forced to say; בית הלל allow even extra things.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית שמאי say: only about what he makes him vow. And בית הלל say: even about what he does not make him vow.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third argument. If the robber demands a certain vow, may the person add extra items to it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית שמאי keep the vow to exactly what was demanded, and anything extra is not covered by the permission. בית הלל let him add more, perhaps to make his words more convincing. The next step gives an example.

keyTerms.meaning: He makes him vow; he forces him to make a vow
About that which he does not

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַדִּירוֹ.
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: only about what he makes him vow.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אַף בַּמֶּה שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַדִּירוֹ.
phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say: even about what he does not make him vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַדִּירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third disagreement, which the next step illustrates.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: only the demanded content is permitted. בית הלל: even added content is permitted.

steps.title: Example: the wife and the children
steps.stepSummary: The משנה illustrates the third argument with a קונם vow that was demanded about his wife, and to which he added his children.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? He said to him: Say, 'קונם that my wife benefits from me,' and he said, 'קונם that my wife and my children benefit from me.' בית שמאי say: his wife is permitted and his children are forbidden. And בית הלל say: both are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains the previous argument with a case. The robber demanded a vow about the wife only, but the man added his children too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The part that was forced (the wife) is not binding according to everyone. בית שמאי say the extra part (the children) was his own free choice, so that vow takes effect and his children may not benefit from him. בית הלל say the whole statement came from the same pressure, so none of it binds.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? This introduces an example
A vow word that makes something forbidden like a קרבן
Benefits from
These and those, meaning both groups

steps.whatToRemember: In all three arguments בית הלל are more lenient. A vow made under pressure to save one's property does not bind, even with a שבועה, even when offered first, and even with added parts.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Forbidden' here does not mean the man sinned by speaking. It means the vow actually took effect, so his children may not benefit from him.

phrases.english: How so? He said to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the robber or extortionist, telling the man what vow to say.

phrases.english: Say: 'Konam, if my wife benefits from me,'
and he said: 'Konam, if my wife and my children benefit from me,'
Beit Shammai say: his wife is permitted
and his children are forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ מוּתָּרִין.
phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say: both these and those are permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד? אָמַר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the third מחלוקת with a concrete case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: the demanded part (wife) is not binding, but the added part (children) is binding. בית הלל: neither part is binding.

steps.title: Challenge: isn't the law of the kingdom binding?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the משנה can permit misleading tax collectors, when שמואל ruled that the law of the kingdom is binding law.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: But didn't שמואל say: the law of the kingdom is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by challenging the משנה's permission to make a misleading vow to tax collectors. It sets up a question that the next lines will need to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה (on the previous דף) listed tax collectors together with robbers. But שמואל holds that a government's laws, including its taxes, are binding according to הלכה. If so, avoiding tax by a misleading vow should be forbidden, so why does the משנה allow it?

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion of the משנה begins here
But didn't he say? This brings a source that seems to contradict
The law of the kingdom is the law; government laws are binding in הלכה

steps.whyThisMatters: דינא דמלכותא דינא is a major הלכה about how a Jew must relate to the laws and taxes of the government.

phrases.english: GEMARA: But didn't Shmuel say:
phrases.notes: The question is aimed at the tax collectors (מוכסין) the משנה mentioned on the previous דף.

phrases.english: The law of the kingdom is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: דִּינָא דְמַלְכוּתָא דִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה to the גמרא's first challenge, aimed at the משנה's opening permission to vow to tax collectors.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's permission to make a misleading vow to tax collectors.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If government law is binding, paying the tax is a real obligation, so dodging it by a misleading vow should not be allowed.

steps.title: The tax collector takes whatever he wants
steps.stepSummary: שמואל himself explains that the משנה is talking about a tax collector who has no fixed rate.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא said in the name of רב כהנא, who said in the name of שמואל: The משנה is talking about a tax collector who has no fixed amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 5. The משנה lets you fool this tax collector because he collects whatever he likes, not a set tax.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דינא דמלכותא דינא only covers real, organized government law. A collector who makes up his own amounts is not carrying out the king's law. He is basically a robber, so you may protect yourself from him.

keyTerms.meaning: Tax collector (customs officer)
A fixed, set amount
The law of the kingdom is binding law

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the limit of דינא דמלכותא דינא: it applies to fair, set government taxes, not to random taking.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא
phrases.english: Rav Ḥinnana said that Rav Kahana said
that Shmuel said:
It refers to a tax collector who has no fixed amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: בְּמוֹכֵס שֶׁאֵין לוֹ קִצְבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to allow fooling any government tax collector, which goes against דינא דמלכותא דינא.
steps.terutzMaskana: It only allows fooling a collector with no fixed rate, who is not following the king's law.

steps.title: The tax collector appointed himself
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי gives a different answer: the collector was never appointed by the government.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי said: The משנה is talking about a tax collector who set himself up on his own.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second answer to the same question from step 5. Here the tax collector has no government authority at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's answer: the collector was appointed but takes unfairly. רבי ינאי's school: the collector was never appointed. Either way, there is no real government law involved, so דינא דמלכותא דינא does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sets himself up on his own (self-appointed)
The school (study house) of רבי ינאי

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai said:
It refers to a tax collector who stands up on his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמַר: בְּמוֹכֵס הָעוֹמֵד מֵאֵלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the same קשיא, alongside step 6
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to be about a government-appointed collector.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is about a collector with no government appointment, so there is no king's law to respect.

steps.title: How can he vow that the produce is the king's?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of vowing that produce belongs to the king, and asks how that vow is worded.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said he may vow that the produce belongs to the king's house, even though it does not. How exactly does he make that vow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה and asks how such a vow would actually be said. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow forbids things on a person. Saying 'this belongs to the king' is a claim, not a vow. So the גמרא wants to know what words turn this claim into a real vow.

keyTerms.meaning: The king's house (the royal household or government)
How does he vow?

phrases.english: That they belong to the house of the king,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינָן שֶׁל בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ.
phrases.english: even though they do not belong to the house of the king.
How does he vow?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי נָדַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new clause of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The actual wording of a vow that his produce belongs to the king

steps.title: The vow forbids all produce if this is not the king's
steps.stepSummary: רב explains the wording: 'May all the produce of the world be forbidden to me if this is not the king's.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עמרם said in the name of רב: He says, 'May the produce of the world be forbidden to me if this is not the king's.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives the wording. The man makes his claim believable by putting a large prohibition on himself if he is lying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow works as a condition: if the produce is not the king's, all produce becomes forbidden to him. The tax collector reasons that no one would risk that, so he believes him.

keyTerms.meaning: They shall be forbidden
All the produce (fruits) of the world

phrases.english: Rav Amram said that Rav said:
When he says: "The produce of the world shall be forbidden to me
if these do not belong to the house of the king."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב עַמְרָם אָמַר רַב: בְּאוֹמֵר ״יֵאָסְרוּ פֵּירוֹת הָעוֹלָם עָלַי אִם אֵינָן שֶׁל בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The vow is a condition: all the world's produce is forbidden to him if this produce is not the king's.

steps.title: But then all produce becomes forbidden to him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the produce really is not the king's, so the condition is met and all produce should become forbidden to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he said 'they shall be forbidden,' all the produce of the world should now be forbidden to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's wording. The condition is actually true, so the vow should take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה allows the vow because it is said under pressure. But a real vow with a condition that came true should still forbid all produce to him for good. That would be a terrible result, so the משנה could not mean this.

keyTerms.meaning: They became forbidden
The produce of the world (Aramaic)

phrases.english: Since he said "they shall be forbidden" —
all the produce of the world becomes forbidden to him!

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּאָמַר ״יֵאָסְרוּ״ אִיתְּסַרוּ עֲלֵיהּ כׇּל פֵּירֵי עָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording given in step 9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The condition (the produce is not the king's) is true, so the vow should take effect and forbid all produce to him forever.

steps.title: He limits the vow to today
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he says the produce is forbidden only 'today.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He says 'today': the produce is forbidden to him only for today.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by limiting the vow to one day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the vow only lasts one day, the damage is small. He goes without produce for a day and then it is over.

keyTerms.meaning: Today

phrases.english: When he says "today."

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאוֹמֵר ״הַיּוֹם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding a detail to the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vow forbids all produce forever.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vow only forbids produce for today.

steps.title: The tax collector won't accept a one-day vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if he says 'today' out loud, the tax collector won't believe him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says 'today,' the tax collector won't accept it from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'today' answer. A one-day vow is too easy to keep, so it would not convince the collector.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point of the vow is to sound so serious that the collector believes him. Giving up produce for one day is not a big deal, so a liar might easily say it. The collector would not be fooled.

keyTerms.meaning: He won't accept it from him

phrases.english: If he says "today,"
the tax collector will not accept it from him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דְּאָמַר ״הַיּוֹם״ לָא מְקַבֵּל מִינֵּיהּ מוֹכֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 11
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A one-day vow is too light to convince the tax collector, so the vow would not do its job.

steps.title: He thinks 'today' but says the vow plainly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: he says 'today' only in his heart, and out loud he says the vow with no time limit.
steps.simpleTranslation: He says 'today' in his heart, and out loud he says the vow with no time limit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא combines both needs. The collector hears a full, serious vow, but in his mind the man limits it to one day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spoken plainly, the vow sounds endless, so the collector believes it. The unspoken 'today' is meant to keep the real prohibition short. The next step deals with whether a thought in his heart can really count.

keyTerms.meaning: In his heart (in his mind)
Says out loud with his lips
Plainly, with no details or limits

phrases.english: When he says "today" in his heart,
and says it with his lips without any limit.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאוֹמֵר בְּלִבּוֹ ״הַיּוֹם״, וּמוֹצִיא בִּשְׂפָתָיו סְתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting what is spoken from what is meant
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He must choose between a vow that lasts forever and a spoken 'today' that won't convince.
steps.terutzMaskana: He speaks the vow plainly but limits it in his mind.

steps.title: Unspoken thoughts count when someone is forced
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits that thoughts in the heart usually don't count, but says that in a case of being forced, it is different.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though we hold that things in the heart are not real words, a case of being forced is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a problem before anyone raises it. Normally a thought you never said has no legal effect, but when someone is forced into a vow, his inner limit does count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual rule, דברים שבלב אינם דברים, should make the unspoken 'today' worthless. But here the man only vowed because the collector pressured him. So we follow what he really meant, and the vow lasts only one day.

keyTerms.meaning: Words in the heart are not words (unspoken thoughts have no legal effect)
Cases where a person is forced or under pressure
It is different

steps.whatToRemember: A vow to fool a tax collector is allowed only when the collector is not carrying out real government law (no fixed rate, or self-appointed). The vow is said out loud with no limit but meant for 'today' only. Because the man is forced, his unspoken limit counts, even though thoughts in the heart normally don't.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the rule דברים שבלב אינם דברים. The rule still stands; being forced is an exception where the inner thought does count.

phrases.english: And even though we hold
that matters in the heart are not matters —
regarding cases of being forced, it is different.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּסְבִירָא לַן דְּבָרִים שֶׁבַּלֵּב אֵינָן דְּבָרִים לְגַבֵּי אוֹנָסִין שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the answer of step 13 against an unstated objection
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The unspoken 'today' should not count, since thoughts in the heart are not words.
steps.terutzMaskana: When a person is forced, his unspoken limit does count.

steps.title: Is the forced vow limited to what the tax collector demands?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: בית שמאי say a person may vow only about what he is forced to vow about. בית הלל say he may vow even about more than that.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: בית שמאי say one may vow with every kind of vow (except a שבועה), and so on. בית שמאי say: he may vow only about what the tax collector makes him vow about. בית הלל say: even about what he does not make him vow about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's lines again. These are the same disagreements between בית שמאי and בית הלל already seen in steps 1, 3 and 4, not a new argument. They are quoted here to set up רב הונא's ברייתא in step 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees a person may make a vow that does not count to save himself from a tax collector. The question is whether he may add to it. בית שמאי limit him to exactly what was demanded. בית הלל let him go further.

keyTerms.meaning: makes him vow (forces him to take a vow)
even
with everything, with every kind of vow

phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: with everything, etc.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַדִּירוֹ,
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: only about what he makes him vow,
phrases.notes: "He" is the tax collector forcing the person to vow.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אַף בְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מַדִּירוֹ.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: even about what he does not make him vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: בַּכֹּל כּוּ׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of the vow 'in the heart' and quotes the משנה's disagreements again (steps 1, 3 and 4) as the heading for the next discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: a forced vow may cover only what was demanded. בית הלל: it may cover even more.

steps.title: Example: adding the children to a vow about the wife
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives an example. The tax collector demands a vow about the wife, and the man adds his children. בית שמאי say the children become forbidden. בית הלל say both are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? The tax collector told him to say: 'קונם, my wife may not benefit from me.' He said: 'קונם, my wife and my children may not benefit from me.' בית שמאי say his wife is permitted and his children are forbidden. בית הלל say both are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains the argument from the step before with a real-life case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For בית שמאי, the wife's part was forced, so it does not count. The children were added by choice, so that part is a real vow. For בית הלל, the whole vow was said under pressure, so none of it counts.

keyTerms.meaning: how so? (introduces an example)
a word used to make something forbidden, like a קרבן
benefits from me
permitted / forbidden

steps.whatToRemember: בית שמאי treat the extra part a person adds on his own as a real vow. בית הלל say the whole vow was made under pressure, so none of it counts.

phrases.english: How so? He said to him:
phrases.notes: The tax collector is the one speaking, telling the man what vow to say.

phrases.english: "Konam: my wife benefiting from me,"
phrases.notes: He means: my wife may not benefit from me if what I say is not true.

phrases.english: and he said: "Konam: my wife and my children benefiting from me."
Beit Shammai say: his wife is permitted
and his children are forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ מוּתָּרִין.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: both these and those are permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an example of the general rule from Step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Adding the children: בית שמאי say they become forbidden, and בית הלל say everyone is permitted.

steps.title: רב הונא's ברייתא: may one offer a שבועה first?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא brings a ברייתא. בית שמאי say the person may not be the first to offer a שבועה. בית הלל say he may.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: a ברייתא teaches that בית שמאי say he may not open with a שבועה, and בית הלל say he may even open with a שבועה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא brings a ברייתא that gives its own version of the משנה's argument about 'opening' (step 2), but it speaks of a שבועה instead of a נדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Opening' means the person offers the oath himself before the tax collector asks for one. בית שמאי forbid this, and בית הלל allow it. This sets up the questions in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: it was taught (introduces a ברייתא)
he will open for him (offer it first, before being asked)
an oath

phrases.english: Rav Huna said: it was taught,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: לֹא יִפְתַּח לוֹ בִּשְׁבוּעָה,
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: he may not open with an oath to him,
phrases.notes: "Open" means he offers the oath on his own, before the tax collector even asks.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אַף יִפְתַּח לוֹ בִּשְׁבוּעָה.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: he may even open with an oath to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: תָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא with another argument between the same two sides about forced vows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: one may not offer a שבועה first. בית הלל: one may.

steps.title: Does the ברייתא imply בית שמאי allow offering a נדר first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the ברייתא closely. If בית שמאי forbid only offering a שבועה first, it sounds like offering a נדר first is fine. But the משנה says בית שמאי forbid offering even a נדר first.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to בית שמאי, it is only with a שבועה that he may not open. That implies he may open with a נדר. But we learned in the משנה that בית שמאי say he may not open with a נדר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a precise reading of the ברייתא and shows that it seems to clash with the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא names only a שבועה. That suggests a נדר is less strict and may be offered first. But the משנה itself says בית שמאי forbid offering even a נדר first, so the two sources seem to disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: this implies, but then
a vow (making an item forbidden), less severe than a שבועה
but we learned (in a משנה)!

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'opening with' a vow (offering it first) with simply 'making' a vow. The משנה allows a forced נדר. Here the question is only about offering one first.

phrases.english: According to Beit Shammai, it is with an oath
that he may not open to him,
which implies that with a vow he may open to him.
But didn't we learn: Beit Shammai say:
he may not open to him with a vow!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא תְּנַן, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: לֹא יִפְתַּח לוֹ בַּנֶּדֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא from Step 17 using a close reading of its wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's version of בית שמאי's view
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By naming only a שבועה, the ברייתא suggests a נדר may be offered first. The משנה says בית שמאי forbid even that.

steps.title: Does the ברייתא imply בית שמאי allow a שבועה when demanded?
steps.stepSummary: A second question: if בית שמאי forbid only offering a שבועה first, it sounds like making one when demanded is fine. But the משנה says בית שמאי forbid a שבועה completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also: it is only opening with a שבועה that he may not do, which implies he may make a vow with a שבועה. But we learned that בית שמאי say one may vow with everything except a שבועה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second close reading of the same ברייתא that also seems to clash with the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא forbids only offering a שבועה first. That suggests a שבועה is allowed if the tax collector demands it. But the משנה says בית שמאי never allow a שבועה in this situation.

keyTerms.meaning: and furthermore (a second question)
to open (offer first)
he does vow (make the vow itself)
except for

phrases.english: And furthermore: it is opening
that he may not open to him with an oath,
which implies he may indeed vow with an oath.
phrases.notes: He means if the tax collector demands the oath, he may make it.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn: Beit Shammai say:
one may vow with everything except with an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ: מִיפְתָּח הוּא דְּלָא יִפְתַּח לוֹ בִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second challenge to the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's version of בית שמאי's view
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By forbidding only offering a שבועה first, the ברייתא suggests a demanded שבועה is allowed. The משנה says בית שמאי forbid a שבועה entirely.

steps.title: Each source shows the strongest form of one side's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the משנה uses a נדר to show how far בית שמאי go. The ברייתא uses a שבועה to show how far בית הלל go.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה taught the case of a נדר to show you the strength of בית שמאי's view. The ברייתא taught the case of a שבועה to show you the strength of בית הלל's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both questions together by explaining why each source chose its case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה shows that בית שמאי forbid offering even a נדר first, which is a big step for them. The ברייתא shows that בית הלל allow offering even a שבועה first, which is a big step for them. So we should not learn anything about בית שמאי from what the ברייתא leaves out, and both questions go away.

keyTerms.meaning: to let you know
the strength of (how far their view goes)
a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא was written to show how far בית הלל go, so it tells us nothing new about בית שמאי. בית שמאי forbid offering even a נדר first, and they never allow a שבועה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common way the גמרא works: a source picks the case that best shows how far one side's opinion reaches. You cannot draw a conclusion about the other side from what that source leaves out.

phrases.english: The Mishna taught it with a vow,
to let you know the strength of Beit Shammai.
The baraita taught it with an oath,
to let you know the strength of Beit Hillel.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא מַתְנִיתִין בְּנֶדֶר, לְהוֹדִיעֲךָ כֹּחָן דְּבֵית שַׁמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers both questions from Steps 18 and 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why each source chose its case: each one shows how far one side's view goes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the ברייתא's wording tells us exactly what בית שמאי allow.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא was written to show how far בית הלל go. בית שמאי forbid offering even a נדר first and forbid a שבועה completely.

steps.title: רב אשי: The ברייתא is about asking for release from an oath
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer. He says the ברייתא is about whether a שבועה can be released by a חכם, not about vows made to tax collectors.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: This is what the ברייתא means. בית שמאי say there is no asking for release from a שבועה. בית הלל say there is asking for release from a שבועה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different way to solve the contradiction between the ברייתא and the משנה. רב אשי moves the ברייתא to a completely different topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer (step 20) kept the ברייתא about tax collectors. רב אשי says the ברייתא is not talking about tax collectors at all. It is about whether a person can go to a חכם and ask to be released from a שבועה. Since the ברייתא and the משנה now deal with two different topics, they no longer contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is teaching. The גמרא uses this to explain what a source really means.
Asking a חכם to release a person from his vow or oath.
An oath.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with step 20. That answer kept the ברייתא about tax collectors. רב אשי takes it to a whole new topic: release from an oath.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: This is what it is teaching:
phrases.notes: 'It' means the ברייתא that רב הונא brought in step 17.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: אֵין שְׁאֵלָה בִּשְׁבוּעָה,
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: There is no asking for release from an oath,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: יֵשׁ שְׁאֵלָה בִּשְׁבוּעָה.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: There is asking for release from an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר, הָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the questions in steps 18-19, different from the answer in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the source: the ברייתא is moved to a different topic, release from oaths.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the ברייתא was about making vows or oaths to tax collectors, so it seemed to contradict the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about whether a חכם can release an oath, so it does not contradict the משנה about tax collectors.

steps.title: New משנה: Saplings or a garment declared a קרבן 'if not' cut or burned
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. If someone says his saplings are a קרבן 'if they are not cut down,' or his garment is a קרבן 'if it is not burned,' the items can be redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If a person says, 'These saplings are a קרבן if they are not cut down,' or 'This garment is a קרבן if it is not burned,' they can be redeemed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It gives a vow that depends on a condition, 'if they are not cut,' and rules that the items can be redeemed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person makes his property holy only if a certain thing does not happen. If the saplings are not cut or the garment is not burned, the items become holy. The משנה says they are like other holy things that can be redeemed with money.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. This marks the start of a new משנה.
Young trees, saplings.
An offering. Saying 'this is a קרבן' makes the item holy.
A garment or cloak.
Redemption: buying back a holy item with money so it becomes ordinary again.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
'These saplings are an offering
if they are not cut down,'
'This garment is an offering
if it is not burned,'
— they can be redeemed.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הֲרֵי נְטִיעוֹת הָאֵלּוּ קׇרְבָּן אִם אֵינָן נִקְצָצוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of the previous one ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When property is declared a קרבן 'if it is not cut or burned,' it can be redeemed.

steps.title: Second wording: a קרבן 'until' they are cut or burned
steps.stepSummary: The משנה starts a second wording: 'These saplings are a קרבן until they are cut down' or 'This garment is a קרבן until it is burned.' The ruling comes in the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person says, 'These saplings are a קרבן until they are cut down,' or 'This garment is a קרבן until it is burned' —
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is setting up a second case with slightly different words. The ruling for this case comes right after this part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only change from step 22 is the word: 'until' (עד) instead of 'if not' (אם אינן). The משנה is showing that this small change in wording can change the law. Watch for the ruling in the next part to see how it differs.

keyTerms.meaning: Until they are cut down.
Until it is burned.

steps.confusionAlert: Read slowly. These lines look almost the same as step 22. The only difference is 'until' instead of 'if not.'

phrases.english: 'These saplings are an offering
until they are cut down,'
'This garment is an offering
until it is burned' —

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי נְטִיעוֹת הָאֵלּוּ קׇרְבָּן עַד שֶׁיִּקָּצְצוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second wording that contrasts with the case in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the 'until' case. The ruling is stated in the continuation of the משנה.
